questiontext.text:
Goal

You write four functions that build tuples of different shapes.

How this works in Python

Java hands you an array when you want a fixed number of values, and a record when those values deserve names.

int[] point = {0, 0};
point[0] = 99;          // compiles, and the array now holds {99, 0}

record Point(int x, int y) {}

The array is fixed in length and wide open to change. Every slot can be written to for as long as the array exists. Python's tuple is fixed in both ways at once.

A tuple is a sequence of values in order, and nothing about it changes after it is built. No slot can be written to, no value can be added, and no value can be removed. Reading works exactly as it does on a list.

point = (0, 0)
print(point[1])       # 0
print(len(point))     # 2
point[0] = 99
# TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment

The comma builds the tuple, not the parentheses

Parentheses only group, the same way they group in arithmetic. (5) is the number five with a pair of parentheses round it. The comma is what makes a tuple, so a tuple holding one value needs a trailing comma.

pair  = 3, 4      # a tuple of two, no parentheses anywhere
plain = (5)       # still the number 5
one   = (5,)      # a tuple of one
also  = 5,        # the same tuple of one

Python prints that trailing comma back at you, so (5,) on screen is how you tell a tuple of one from a number wearing parentheses. Type the comma by accident at the end of a return line and you hand the caller a tuple where a number was expected. That mistake reads as a typo and lands as a type error a long way downstream, so meet it on purpose now.

A tuple is not a list of fixed length

A list holding two items still allows readings[0] = 99. The tuple refuses. That refusal is the whole point, because it lets a tuple stand for one thing made of parts, such as a coordinate or a row read from a file, rather than a collection you intend to work on.

The tuple built-in converts any sequence in one call, so tuple([1, 2, 3]) gives (1, 2, 3) and leaves the original list alone.

Your task

Write four functions. Each one returns a value and none of them prints.

  • origin() takes no arguments and returns a tuple of two zeros.
  • solo(value) returns a tuple holding value and nothing else.
  • grouped(value) returns (value), parentheses and all. Work out its type before you run it.
  • freeze(items) takes a list and returns a tuple of the same items in the same order.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text exactly.

Rules
  • Build the tuple of one with a trailing comma. Do not call tuple for it.
  • Write no square brackets anywhere. No list literal and no indexing.
  • Convert the list in one call. No loop.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

No AI. Type every character yourself. This tier builds the muscle, and a tool that types it for you skips the exercise.

testcode.text: import inspect whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (origin, solo, grouped, freeze)) assert "[" not in whole, "rule broken: no square brackets, build tuples" assert "for " not in whole, "rule broken: the tuple built-in converts the whole list in one call" assert "tuple(" not in inspect.getsource(solo), "rule broken: a trailing comma builds the tuple of one" print(freeze([])) print(solo(None)) print(len(solo(origin()))) print(origin() + solo(9)) point = origin() try: point[0] = 99 except TypeError as problem: print("TypeError:", problem)

expected.text: () (None,) 1 (0, 0, 9) TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment

questiontext.text:
Goal

You write four functions that unpack pairs, lines and characters instead of indexing them.

How this works in Python

Java pulls a pair apart one index at a time and names each piece on a line of its own.

for (Object[] pair : pairs) {
    String site = (String) pair[0];
    int count   = (int) pair[1];
    ...
}

Python takes the whole shape apart in one statement. Writing several names on the left of an assignment with a sequence on the right is called unpacking, and Python binds each name to the value sitting in the matching position.

site, count = ("Kaitaia", 42)
print(site)     # Kaitaia
print(count)    # 42

The parentheses on the right are optional, as they always are round a tuple. Unpacking works on any sequence rather than only on tuples, so a list unpacks and so does a string.

a, b, c = "xyz"
print(b)        # y

The count has to match, and Python checks it while the program runs

Ask for two names from a three-item tuple and you get ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2). Ask for four and you get ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 4, got 3). Java catches that mistake while it compiles, so this is a whole class of defect you now have to catch in review and in tests instead.

One name may carry a star, and it collects whatever is left over

The starred name always becomes a list, even when there is nothing left for it to collect.

*body, footer = ["alpha", "beta", "END"]
print(body)     # ['alpha', 'beta']
print(footer)   # END

*body, footer = ["END"]
print(body)     # []

A statement may hold one starred name at most, and the sequence still has to be long enough to fill the plain names. Unpacking an empty list into *body, footer raises ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected at least 1, got 0), because footer has nothing to bind to.

A value you do not want still needs a name

Python has no way to skip a position, so the convention is a single underscore. _ is an ordinary name that reads as "I am ignoring this one", and reviewers read it the same way. The same underscore may appear more than once in one statement.

_, middle, _ = "abc"
print(middle)   # b

A for loop unpacks in its header

Whatever the loop hands you is taken apart on the spot, which deletes the three lines of naming the Java version needs.

pairs = [("Kaitaia", 42), ("Otautahi", 7)]
for site, count in pairs:
    print(f"{site}: {count}")
Your task

Write four functions. Each one returns a value and none of them prints.

  • pair_labels(pairs) takes a list of (site, count) tuples and returns a list of strings, one per pair, each in the form Kaitaia: 42. Unpack in the loop header and build each string with an f-string.
  • total_count(pairs) takes the same list and returns the counts added together. The site is a value you do not want.
  • strip_footer(lines) takes a list whose last line is a footer and returns a list of everything before it. A list holding the footer alone comes back as an empty list.
  • middle_char(code) takes a string of exactly three characters and returns the middle one, without indexing.

An empty list of pairs is an ordinary input for the first two functions. Work out what each of them should return before you run anything.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text exactly.

Rules
  • Do not index. No [0], no [1], no [-1]. Unpack instead.
  • Unpack in the for header. Pulling the pair apart on the next line is the Java shape.
  • Drop the footer with a starred name. No slicing, no len, no range, no pop.
  • Name a value you do not want _.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI for explanation only. Ask it what an error means or why one form is more idiomatic. Do not let it write your answer.

testcode.text: import inspect whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (pair_labels, total_count, strip_footer, middle_char)) for banned in ("[0]", "[1]", "[2]", "[-1]", "[-2]", "[:", "len(", "range(", ".pop("): assert banned not in whole, "rule broken: unpack instead of indexing, slicing or counting" def for_target(function): headers = [line.strip() for line in inspect.getsource(function).splitlines() if line.strip().startswith("for ")] assert headers, "rule broken: loop over the pairs with a for statement" return headers[0][4:headers[0].index(" in ")] assert "," in for_target(pair_labels), "rule broken: unpack in the for header" assert "," in for_target(total_count), "rule broken: unpack in the for header" assert "_" in for_target(total_count), "rule broken: name the site you do not want _" assert "*" in inspect.getsource(strip_footer), "rule broken: one starred name collects the body" print(pair_labels([])) print(total_count([])) try: print(strip_footer([])) except ValueError as problem: print("ValueError:", problem) try: print(pair_labels([("Kaitaia", 42, 3)])) except ValueError as problem: print("ValueError:", problem) print(middle_char("xyz") + middle_char("123"))

expected.text: [] 0 ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected at least 1, got 0) ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2) y2

questiontext.text:
Goal

You write six functions that return several values at once and unpack them again.

How this works in Python

Java needs a type to carry three values out of a method, and a spare variable to swap two.

record Summary(int low, int high, double mean) {}

Summary summarise(List<Integer> readings) { ... }

int temp = a;
a = b;
b = temp;

Python needs neither. The comma builds a tuple, which is a fixed sequence of values in order. You cannot add to a tuple or change one of its items once it exists. Parentheses around a tuple only group it and are usually left out.

def summarise(readings):
    return min(readings), max(readings), sum(readings) / len(readings)

low, high, mean = summarise([4, 9, 2, 7])
print(low, high, mean)          # 2 9 5.5

The return line builds a three-item tuple. The line after it takes that tuple apart and binds each item to a name. Taking a sequence apart into names is called unpacking, and it works on any sequence, not only tuples.

Four more forms carry the rest of the lesson.

  • left, right = right, left swaps two names in one statement. Python builds the whole right-hand side first, then binds, so no temporary variable exists.
  • head, *tail = readings binds the first item to head. The star marks the name that collects everything left over, so tail becomes a list of the rest.
  • first, *middle, last = readings takes both ends and gathers the rest in the middle. One statement may hold one starred name at most.
  • (site, channel), value = record unpacks a nested structure in one statement. The shape on the left mirrors the shape on the right.

Unpacking checks the count at run time. Ask for two names from a three-item tuple and Python raises ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2). Ask for four and it raises ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 4, got 3). Java catches that mistake at compile time, so watch for it in review here.

One more form has no Java counterpart at all. A trailing comma builds a tuple of one.

x = 5,
print(x)          # (5,)

You can type that comma by accident at the end of a return line. The result is a one-item tuple where you expected a number. Meet it on purpose now so you recognise it later.

Your task

Write six functions. Each one returns a value and none of them prints.

  • summarise(readings) returns the smallest value, the largest value and the mean, in that order. Use the built-in functions min, max and sum.
  • swapped(left, right) swaps the two names, then returns both in the new order.
  • split_head(readings) returns the first item and a list of everything after it.
  • split_ends(readings) returns the first item, a list of the middle, and the last item.
  • unpack_record(record) takes a nested record such as (("A1", 3), 12.5) and returns the site, the channel and the value as three separate items.
  • one_tuple() returns the value that x = 5, produces.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character, brackets and commas included.

Rules
  • Do not index. No [0], no [1], no [-1]. Unpack instead of subscripting.
  • Build no class, record or holder object to carry three values home.
  • Swap the two names in one statement. No temporary variable, and no name containing temp or tmp.
  • Return a bare comma-separated expression. Do not wrap the returned tuple in parentheses.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.

testcode.text: low, high, mean = summarise([4, 9, 2, 7]) print(low, high, mean) print(summarise([3])) print(swapped("north", "south"))

head, tail = split_head([10, 20, 30, 40]) print(head, tail) first, middle, last = split_ends([10, 20, 30, 40]) print(first, middle, last) print(split_ends([1, 2])) print(unpack_record((("A1", 3), 12.5))) value = one_tuple() print(value, type(value))

import inspect whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (summarise, swapped, split_head, split_ends, unpack_record, one_tuple)) for banned in ("[0]", "[1]", "[2]", "[-1]", "[-2]"): assert banned not in whole, "rule broken: unpack instead of subscripting" assert "class " not in whole, "rule broken: no holder object" assert "return (" not in whole, "rule broken: return a bare comma-separated expression" assert "temp" not in whole and "tmp" not in whole, "rule broken: swap without a temporary" body = inspect.getsource(swapped).strip().splitlines() assert len(body) <= 3, "rule broken: swap in a single statement" try: a, b = summarise([1, 2, 3]) except ValueError as problem: print("ValueError:", problem) try: a, b, c, d = summarise([1, 2, 3]) except ValueError as problem: print("ValueError:", problem) print(unpack_record((("Z9", 0), 0.0))) print(one_tuple() + one_tuple())

expected.text: ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2) ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 4, got 3) ('Z9', 0, 0.0) (5, 5)
